Note that $X,Y\in\mathfrak{g}_{x,0}$ if and only if $\mathrm{val}(X_{\alpha})\geq-\alpha(x)$ and $\mathrm{val}(Y_{\alpha})\geq\alpha(x)$ for all $\alpha$ . We observe from Table 2 that our representatives satisfy $\mathrm{val}(Y_{\alpha})=-\mathrm{val}(X_{\alpha})$ for all $\alpha$ . Hence these were optimally chosen: ${\mathrm{d}\phi}_{\Gamma}\in\mathfrak{g}_{x,0}$ if and only if

$$ \alpha(x)=-\mathrm{val}(X_{\alpha}),\quad\forall\alpha\in\Phi_{X}. $$

We claim this system of equations is consistent, whereby the solution is an affine subspace $\mathcal{A}_{\Gamma}$ which is a union of facets of $\mathcal{A}$ . In this case we’ll let $\mathcal{F}$ be any maximal facet of $\mathcal{A}_{\Gamma}$ ; note that $\dim(\mathcal{F})=\dim(\mathcal{A}_{\Gamma})$ .

To solve (7.1) explicitly, let $\tilde{\Gamma}$ be the partition of the set $\{1,2,\cdots,m\}$ induced by the partition $\Gamma$ ; that is, for each $\gamma\in\Gamma$ the element $\tilde{\gamma}\in\tilde{\Gamma}$ is the set of indices of the Witt basis $B_{\gamma}$ attached to $V_{\gamma}$ . For each $\gamma\in\Gamma$ , the roots $\alpha\in\Phi_{X|_{V_{\gamma}}}$ are linear combinations of $\{\varepsilon_{i}\mid i\in\tilde{\gamma}\}$ . The linear system (7.1) can thus be decoupled into $|\Gamma|$ distinct linear systems, whence any solution may be written $x=\sum_{\tilde{\gamma}\in\tilde{\Gamma}}x_{\tilde{\gamma}}$ as each $x_{\tilde{\gamma}}$ runs over an affine set $\mathcal{A}_{\tilde{\gamma}}$ . Let $e_{\tilde{\gamma}}$ be the vector such that $\varepsilon_{i}(e_{\tilde{\gamma}})=1$ for all $i\in\tilde{\gamma}$ and $0$ otherwise.

It is then a straightforward exercise to see that solving these uncoupled systems (with notation of the corresponding paragraphs in Section 5) yields

$$ \mathcal{A}_{\tilde{\gamma}}=\begin{cases}\mathbb{R}e_{\tilde{\gamma}}&\text{if $\gamma\in\Gamma_{\textsf{{even}}}\cup\Gamma_{\textsf{{hyp}}}$},\\
\{-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{val}(r)e_{\tilde{\gamma}}\}&\text{if $\gamma\in\Gamma_{\textsf{{pairs}}}\cup\Gamma_{\textsf{{quad}}}\cup\Gamma_{\textsf{{trip}}}$},\\

We conclude that $\dim(\mathcal{A}_{\Gamma})=\dim(\mathcal{F})=|\Gamma_{\textsf{{even}}}|+|\Gamma_{\textsf{{hyp}}}|$ , proving the final statement of the proposition.

Now suppose that $\lambda$ is very even, so that there are two $\mathrm{SO}(q)$ -orbits. The first is constructed as in Section 5.3. Since $\Gamma=\Gamma_{\textsf{{even}}}$ consists entirely of pairs, it has size $\dim(\mathcal{F})=\frac{1}{2}|\mathcal{I}_{\lambda}|=\frac{1}{2}|\lambda|$ , which gives the stated dimension for the first $\mathrm{SO}(q)$ -orbit. The second $\mathrm{SO}(q)$ -orbit is obtained by modifying the choice of $X|_{V_{\gamma}}$ on one $\gamma\in\Gamma_{\textsf{{even}}}$ with an expression of the form (5.17). The corresponding linear system consistent, with solution space $\mathbb{R}\tilde{e}$ where $\varepsilon_{j}(\tilde{e})=0$ if $j\notin\tilde{\gamma}$ , $\varepsilon_{j}(\tilde{e})=1$ if $1\leq j<i$ , and $\varepsilon_{i}(\tilde{e})=-1$ . As the solution to this subsystem is again one-dimensional, the dimension of the facet is the same for both orbits attached to $\lambda$ . ∎

Recall that by definition, a pair $\gamma=\{(j_{t},m),(j_{t},m^{\prime})\}$ in $\Gamma_{\textsf{{hyp}}}$ corresponds to a hyperbolic plane in $q_{j_{t}}$ . Therefore to maximize $|\Gamma_{\textsf{{even}}}|+|\Gamma_{\textsf{{hyp}}}|$ over all partitions $\Gamma$ of $\mathcal{I}_{\lambda}$ is to choose a partition which contain all such hyperbolic planes, and all the even parts, from $\mathcal{I}_{\lambda}$ . Then $\mathcal{I}_{\lambda}\setminus(\Gamma_{\textsf{{even}}}\cup\Gamma_{\textsf{{hyp}}})$ has precisely $\sum_{i=1}^{s}\dim\overline{q_{j_{i}}}$ elements, corresponding to the anisotropic kernels of all of the quadratic forms in $\mathsf{q}$ . Complete this to a partition ${\Gamma_{\textrm{max}}}$ of $\mathcal{I}_{\lambda}$ satisfying Proposition 5.1.

#### Theorem 7.2.

Let $(\lambda,\mathsf{q})\in\mathcal{N}(\overline{q},n)$ or $\mathcal{N}^{hyp}(n)$ , and ${\Gamma_{\textrm{max}}}$ a partition of $\mathcal{I}_{\lambda}$ as above. Then the corresponding pair $(\mathcal{F}_{\Gamma_{\textrm{max}}},X_{\Gamma_{\textrm{max}}})$ is distinguished. Its associativity class is the unique one attached to the rational nilpotent orbit $G\cdot X_{\Gamma_{\textrm{max}}}$ by the DeBacker correspondence, for $G=\mathrm{O}(q)$ or $G=\mathrm{SO}(q)$ .

#### Proof.

Since for each $\Gamma$ , each pair in $\Gamma_{\textsf{{even}}}\cup\Gamma_{\textsf{{hyp}}}$ contributes one linear degree of freedom to the solution space $\mathcal{A}_{\Gamma}$ , we conclude that for our choice of $\Gamma={\Gamma_{\textrm{max}}}$ that

$$ \dim(\mathcal{F}_{\Gamma_{\textrm{max}}})=\frac{1}{2}\left(|\lambda|-\sum_{i=1}^{s}\dim\overline{q_{j_{i}}}\right). $$

On the other hand, by Theorem 6.1 we have $\dim(\mathcal{B}({\mathrm{d}\phi}))=\dim(\mathcal{B}(G^{\phi}))$ , which is equal to the split rank of $G^{\phi}$ . The split rank of $\mathrm{U}(M^{i},\gamma^{i})$ is exactly the maximal number of orthogonal hyperbolic planes in $\gamma^{i}$ ; for $i$ odd this is therefore $\frac{1}{2}(\deg(\gamma^{i})-\dim\overline{\gamma^{i}})$ . We deduce from (3.3) that

$$ \dim(\mathcal{F}_{\Gamma_{\textrm{max}}})=\dim(\mathcal{B}({\mathrm{d}\phi})), $$

so the facet is indeed distinguished, as required. ∎

This theorem establishes a constructive map from the classical partition-based parametrization of nilpotent orbits of orthogonal and special orthogonal groups to the building-based parametrization proposed by DeBacker.
